name: Expense Fraud
title: Expense Fraud
answer: Expense fraud covers duplicate claims, inflated amounts, personal costs submitted as business expenses, fictitious receipts, and collusion between employees and approvers or vendors. In an AI accounting context, the scope includes monitoring employee expense reports, corporate card transactions, travel bookings, and invoice submissions for patterns that indicate deliberate misreporting rather than simple error. The work also extends to forensic reconstruction of how a scheme operated, so that findings can support internal investigation and, where needed, external reporting.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Expense fraud covers duplicate claims, inflated amounts, personal costs submitted as business expenses, fictitious receipts, and collusion between employees and approvers or vendors. In an AI accounting context, the scope includes monitoring employee expense reports, corporate card transactions, travel bookings, and invoice submissions for patterns that indicate deliberate misreporting rather than simple error. The work also extends to forensic reconstruction of how a scheme operated, so that findings can support internal investigation and, where needed, external reporting.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The detection layer typically sits on top of existing expense management, ERP, and corporate card systems, pulling structured transaction data and receipt images through APIs or batch exports. Receipts are processed with optical character recognition to extract merchant, date, amount, and line-item detail, while card feeds provide a second view of the same spend. The data is normalized into a common store, often a cloud data warehouse or lake, where employee, approver, department, and vendor identifiers are linked. Models and rules then run either on a scheduled basis or in near real time as claims are submitted.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Most programs combine explicit rules, such as duplicate invoice numbers or amounts just below approval thresholds, with statistical anomaly detection that flags spending far outside an employee's or peer group's normal pattern. Graph techniques are used to find shared bank accounts, addresses, or vendor relationships that suggest collusion, and image analysis can spot altered or reused receipts. Supervised models trained on confirmed fraud cases score new claims, while unsupervised methods surface unusual clusters without needing labeled history. Every flag carries the underlying evidence and a plain-language reason so that auditors can review it efficiently.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Expense data contains personal information, including locations, meal companions, and sometimes medical or family details, so access is restricted, logged, and limited to staff with a defined investigative role. Automated flags are treated as leads, not findings, and any action that affects an employee's pay or employment requires human review and documented justification. Model versions, training data, and decision thresholds are retained so that a specific alert can be reconstructed later for audit, employment dispute, or court. False positives are tracked by outcome, and rules are adjusted when they consistently misclassify legitimate spending.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward earlier intervention, with systems checking receipts and policy compliance at the moment of submission or even before a purchase is approved, rather than after reimbursement. Receipt verification is becoming more capable of detecting edited images and mismatched metadata, while spend data is increasingly linked across travel, procurement, and expense systems to expose patterns that single silos miss. Synthetic fraud examples are being used to train models where real confirmed cases are scarce, and explanations are becoming more detailed so that auditors can see not just what was flagged but why. Over time, the role of the system is shifting from retrospective detection to continuous, evidence-backed monitoring.
